notes.source_note: NVIDIA, [*CUDA Programming Guide*, §1.2.1, “Heterogeneous Systems”](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/01-introduction/programming-model.html#heterogeneous-systems), defines host, device and kernel launches; [§2.6, “Unified and System Memory”](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/02-basics/understanding-memory.html), explains memory access and migration. Data can remain on the device between kernels; unified or remotely accessible memory does not require an explicit whole-array copy before each launch. Device-side launches are also possible. “Control plane” and “compute path” describe the typical division here, not a rule that GPUs never make control decisions. NVIDIA's [Blackwell overview](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/technologies/blackwell-architecture/) describes Grace's NVLink-C2C connection at 900 GB/s bidirectional bandwidth; it is distinct from both the link joining the two GPU dies and GPU-to-GPU NVLink.

notes.limits: Kernel means a function executed by many threads. The host/device split is typical, not a prohibition on GPU control flow or device-side launches. Unified/system memory changes placement and migration, not the physical cost of access. Grace C2C is distinct from intra-GPU NV-HBI and inter-GPU NVLink.

notes.source_note: Samuel Williams, Andrew Waterman and David Patterson, [“Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures”](https://doi.org/10.1145/1498765.1498785), *Communications of the ACM* 52(4) (2009): 65–76, especially pp. 66–67 ([paper](https://aiichironakano.github.io/cs596/Williams-Roofline-CACM09.pdf)). This is a bound using a specified arithmetic mode and memory boundary; $P$ here measures operations per second, not electrical power. NVIDIA's [Blackwell datasheet](https://dam-cdn.nvd.orangelogic.com/AssetLink/y441155802qub41q118b2852i557jem5.pdf), p. 8, lists B200 FP8 throughput of 9 PFLOPS with sparsity, half that for dense work, and 7.7 TB/s of HBM bandwidth: $4.5\times10^{15}/(7.7\times10^{12})\approx584$ operations per byte. The text rounds the bandwidth to about 8 TB/s. The batch-one estimate counts only a multiply and an add per one-byte streamed weight; activations, attention/KV-cache traffic, scale metadata and other operations add work and transfers. Matrix element counts are not transfer counts: finite on-chip storage can require reloads. These are explanatory estimates, not measured application speeds.
notes.claim: Roofline bound, precision-dependent ridge, matrix element/traffic counts and batch-one example
notes.locator: Williams et al. original CACM article pp.66–67, formula/upper-bound discussion; NVIDIA Blackwell datasheet p.8 and sparse/dense footnote; NVIDIA matrix guide §§2–2.1.
notes.verification: Relevant primary passages and metadata checked; arithmetic independently calculated where stated.
notes.limits: Original formula checked as a bound. Independently computed dense FP8 ridge 4.5e15/7.7e12 ≈584, or 562.5 using rounded 8 TB/s. The two-operations-per-byte figure is weight-only for streamed 8-bit matrix-vector arithmetic at batch one, not a complete model-performance forecast. Distinct matrix elements do not measure total traffic.
